title: Mumbai Flights Soar: Fares Spike 40% Ahead of Summer
excerpt: Air India slashes 100+ long-haul routes as jet fuel costs hit 60% of operating expenses, squeezing summer travellers hard.
body:
Mumbai's Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj International Airport is heading into its most expensive summer travel season in recent memory, as a combustible mix of surging jet fuel prices and reduced flight capacity drives international fares sharply higher in May 2026.

**What happened — Air India cuts and a capacity crunch:**
Air India is trimming close to 100 long-haul flights through July 2026, with ripple effects already felt by passengers planning trips across Europe, North America, and Australia. Aviation turbine fuel has surged dramatically, at times accounting for nearly 60 per cent of an airline's operating expenses — far above the usual range. The rising cost of aviation turbine fuel (ATF) has become one of the primary factors behind these service reductions, with ATF prices rising by Rs 73 per litre due to ongoing global tensions.

**Why fares are soaring — the fuel shock behind the numbers:**
Prices of jet fuel have risen more than 80 per cent since the US and Israel launched their war on Iran in late February, prompting airlines to hike fares, reduce their schedules, or both. As displaced passengers turn to other carriers — Emirates, Qatar Airways, Lufthansa, Singapore Airlines — fares are climbing, with prices on some routes jumping between 20 and 40 per cent for summer travel. IATA Director General Willie Walsh said, 'There is no way airlines can absorb it,' adding that carriers are increasing fares and adjusting routes.

**What to watch — no relief on the horizon:**
Analysts say high fares are unlikely to ease soon, with experts warning that prices are likely to stay 'historically elevated for months, not weeks,' meaning travellers should expect expensive tickets well into the summer season. On high-demand international routes such as India to the US or Europe, airlines are cutting daily flights down to four or five times a week to ensure aircraft fly at full capacity.
